blocks.recap_md: Introduces two primality tests to compare (one Θ(√n), one Θ(log n)), then gives `smallest-divisor`/`find-divisor`/`divides?`, which search for a number's smallest divisor by trying successive integers starting at 2.
`prime?` reduces to checking whether n equals its own smallest divisor; the search only needs to go up to √n, since any non-prime n must have a divisor no larger than that, giving Θ(√n) growth.

The faster test rests on Fermat's Little Theorem: for prime n and any positive integer a < n, a raised to the n-th power is congruent to a modulo n; the Fermat test flips this around, picking a random a and using the congruence as evidence (not proof) of primality.

`expmod` computes a base raised to a power, modulo m, efficiently via successive squaring (echoing the earlier fast-expt trick), so its step count grows logarithmically in the exponent rather than linearly.
`fermat-test` picks a random a and checks the Fermat congruence via `expmod`; `fast-prime?` repeats this some number of times, declaring n prime only if every trial passes.

Unlike prior deterministic algorithms, the Fermat test only gives a probably-correct answer - failing proves non-primality, but passing never quite guarantees it, since rare 'Carmichael' numbers fool every base; unfoolable variants exist whose error probability can be driven arbitrarily low with more trials, motivating the broader field of probabilistic algorithms.

Exercise 1.21 asks to try `smallest-divisor` on a few numbers; Exercise 1.22 introduces a `timed-prime-test` harness (using `runtime`) for empirically checking whether prime-testing time actually scales the way the Θ(√n) analysis predicts.

Exercise 1.23 asks to skip even test-divisors above 2 to roughly halve the work and see if runtime improves as predicted; Exercise 1.24 asks to time the Fermat-based `fast-prime?` instead and check whether its growth looks logarithmic.
Exercise 1.25 asks whether Alyssa's simpler `expmod`, which just calls a general fast-exponentiation procedure and takes the remainder at the end, would work just as well in practice.
Exercise 1.26 describes Louis's bug: rewriting `expmod`'s squaring step as an explicit multiplication (calling `expmod` twice) accidentally turns the logarithmic-time process into a linear one.

Exercise 1.27 asks to verify that Carmichael numbers really do fool the Fermat test on every base; Exercise 1.28 introduces the stronger Miller-Rabin test, which can detect a nontrivial square root of 1 during the squaring step to catch non-primality with certainty in more cases.

knowledge_items.statement: Finding a number's smallest divisor via trial division only needs to test candidate divisors up to √n, since any non-prime n must have a divisor no larger than √n; this gives `find-divisor`/`smallest-divisor`/`prime?` an order of growth of Θ(√n) rather than Θ(n).
Fermat's Little Theorem states that if n is prime and a is any positive integer less than n, then a raised to the n-th power is congruent to a modulo n.

The Fermat test exploits Fermat's Little Theorem probabilistically: it picks a random a < n and checks the congruence using `expmod`, which runs in Θ(log n) steps via successive squaring; `fast-prime?` repeats this trial several times, declaring n prime only if every trial passes.

The Fermat test is a genuinely different kind of algorithm from the deterministic ones seen so far: failing the test proves n is not prime, but passing it - even many times - is never a certainty, only very strong evidence, because rare numbers (Carmichael numbers) satisfy the congruence for every base despite not being prime.

Unfoolable variants of the Fermat test (like Miller-Rabin) can have their error probability driven arbitrarily close to zero by running more independent trials, because one can prove the failure condition holds for most bases whenever n is composite - a guarantee the plain Fermat test lacks, since rare numbers (Carmichael numbers) satisfy its congruence for every base despite being composite.

questions.prompt: In `find-divisor`, why does the terminating test check `(> (square test-divisor) n)` rather than `(> test-divisor n)`?
options: Because if n has no divisor less than or equal to √n, it can have no divisor at all up to n, so the search can safely stop at √n instead of n, cutting the work from Θ(n) to Θ(√n)
Because squaring test-divisor is required to avoid an infinite loop inside Scheme's `cond`
Because Scheme's `cond` cannot express a direct comparison between two un-squared numbers
Because n is always a perfect square, so squaring test-divisor is the only meaningful way to compare it
questions.explanation: Any non-prime n must have a divisor no larger than √n, so if none is found among test-divisors up to √n, n must be prime. Squaring test-divisor and comparing to n is exactly the same as comparing test-divisor to √n, which is what shrinks the search space from n down to √n.

questions.prompt: According to Fermat's Little Theorem as stated in this section, if n is prime and a is any positive integer less than n, which relation must hold?
options: a raised to the n-th power is congruent to a modulo n
a raised to the (n-1)-th power is congruent to 1 modulo n
a raised to the n-th power is congruent to n modulo a
n raised to the a-th power is congruent to a modulo n
questions.explanation: The theorem as introduced here is: a^n is congruent to a modulo n. (The exponent n-1 with result 1 is a different, equivalent-looking form used later for Miller-Rabin - it's easy to mix the two up, but this section's statement uses exponent n and result a.)

questions.prompt: Why does `expmod` compute a^n mod m in Θ(log n) steps instead of Θ(n)?
options: It uses successive squaring: whenever the exponent is even, it makes one recursive call on half the exponent and squares that single result, so the exponent roughly halves at each step
Because `remainder` is a constant-time primitive, so the size of the exponent has no effect on the number of steps at all
Because Scheme provides a special hardware instruction for modular exponentiation that `expmod` invokes directly
Because it recurses by multiplying by `base` exactly once for every even value the exponent passes through
questions.explanation: Just like `fast-expt` in 1.2.4, halving the exponent at each even step means the number of recursive calls is proportional to log2(exponent), giving Θ(log n) growth instead of the Θ(n) growth of a straightforward repeated-multiplication approach.

questions.prompt: What does `fast-prime?` (called with n and a trial count `times`) actually return, and why?
options: True only if `fermat-test` succeeds on every one of the `times` independent random trials - a single failed trial is enough to make it return false
True if `fermat-test` succeeds on at least half of the `times` trials
True automatically whenever `times` is greater than zero, regardless of any trial's outcome
The numeric average of the `times` individual test results, rounded to true or false
questions.explanation: `fast-prime?` recurses only as long as `fermat-test` keeps succeeding, and returns false the moment a single trial fails, or true once all `times` trials have passed - matching the Fermat test's asymmetry where any single failure is decisive but successes only accumulate confidence.

questions.prompt: Why is the Fermat test described as differing 'in character' from most familiar algorithms studied so far in the book?
options: Because failing the test proves n is not prime, but passing it - even repeatedly - is never a logical guarantee that n is prime, only very strong evidence, unlike deterministic algorithms whose answers are always exactly correct
Because the Fermat test is the first algorithm in the book that uses recursion
Because the Fermat test cannot be implemented without an external physical source of true randomness
Because unlike other algorithms in the book, the Fermat test's running time cannot be analyzed using order-of-growth notation
questions.explanation: The text's point is the asymmetry between disproof and confirmation: a failed trial is certain proof of non-primality, but passing many trials is still not an absolute guarantee, because rare Carmichael numbers satisfy the congruence for every base. (The Fermat test's own running time is perfectly well described by Θ(log n), so that isn't what makes it different.)

questions.prompt: What is the key advantage of 'unfoolable' variants of the Fermat test (such as Miller-Rabin), compared with the plain Fermat test?
options: For these variants, one can prove that for any composite n the special condition fails for at least half of all possible choices of a, so more trials strictly and provably drive the error probability toward zero - a guarantee the plain Fermat test lacks because of numbers like the Carmichael numbers that fool it on every base
These variants eliminate randomness entirely, deterministically checking every possible value of a
These variants only work correctly for numbers below some fixed size limit, unlike the plain Fermat test
These variants run in Θ(n) time, trading away the plain Fermat test's Θ(log n) speed in exchange for reliability
questions.explanation: The text states that for these variants one can prove the condition fails for most a whenever n is composite, so each additional random trial provably increases confidence; the plain Fermat test has no such guarantee because rare numbers exist that satisfy its congruence for every base.

exercises.hint_md: Just apply `smallest-divisor` directly to each of the three numbers. Think about what it means when the returned divisor equals the number itself, versus when it doesn't.

Build `search-for-primes` on top of `timed-prime-test`, walking consecutive odd integers upward from the given starting point (you can skip even candidates outright, since no even number above 2 is prime). Keep a running count of primes found so you know when to stop after three. When comparing timings across the four ranges, remember you're checking whether the *ratios* between them roughly match what Θ(√n) predicts, not the absolute numbers.

Define `next` as a small dispatch on its input (special-case 2, otherwise add 2), then thread it into `find-divisor`'s recursive call in place of `(+ test-divisor 1)`. When the measured speedup comes out less clean than exactly 2x, consider what other costs `find-divisor` pays on every step that don't scale down just because the divisor sequence got shorter.

Swap in `fast-prime?` (with a fixed trial count) wherever your timing harness currently calls `prime?`. Since Θ(log n) grows so much more slowly than Θ(√n), think about roughly how many more log-steps a million-scale n needs versus a thousand-scale n, and compare that predicted ratio to what you actually measure.

Trace through what each version of `expmod` actually computes at each recursive step, not just what it returns mathematically. Pay attention to the size of the intermediate numbers each version has to construct and operate on along the way.

Sketch the recursion tree for one call to each version of `expmod`. Count how many recursive calls get made at each successive halving of the exponent, and compare what happens to that count when a computed value is reused (via `square`) versus when the identical computation is simply issued again from scratch.

You'll need a procedure that, given n, exhaustively checks the Fermat congruence for every a from 1 up to n − 1, rather than sampling a random a the way `fermat-test` does. Run it on each Carmichael number and see what it reports.

Modify the squaring branch of `expmod` so that, before returning a squared-and-reduced value, it checks whether the value being squared is a nontrivial square root of 1 modulo n (not congruent to 1 or n − 1, yet its square is congruent to 1). The text's own suggestion is to have `expmod` signal this discovery by returning 0; build your Miller-Rabin test to watch for that signal instead of just comparing a final result to `a`.
